title: Find the Flaw
blurb: Real ASP.NET Core snippets, one security flaw each. Find the offending line, then pick the fix a security reviewer would sign off on. Each term is explained as it comes up.

levels.title: L1 · The file download
levels.prompt: Which line is the flaw, and the fix? (path traversal — escaping the intended folder)
levels.hint: Follow the untrusted value to where it's used. What stops it from containing "../"?

payload.intro: An endpoint that returns a file from a downloads folder.

fixes.label: Resolve the full path and verify it still starts under _downloads (else reject)
URL-encode the file name before using it
Wrap the read in a try/catch

levels.explain: Path.Combine doesn't sandbox anything — name = "..\..\appsettings.json" resolves outside _downloads (path traversal). Resolve the absolute path (Path.GetFullPath) and confirm it still lives under _downloads before opening it; better yet, map an allowlist of ids to real files.

failStates.title: Reading the file isn't the flaw
failStates.explain: ReadAllBytes is fine once the path is trusted. The flaw is the line that builds an unchecked path from user input.

failStates.title: Encoding is the wrong tool
failStates.explain: URL-encoding is for URLs/HTML output, not file paths. The fix is to verify the resolved path stays inside the intended folder.

failStates.title: A try/catch hides the symptom
failStates.explain: Catching errors doesn't stop the traversal — the attacker's file is still read. You must constrain the path.

levels.title: L2 · The diagnostics endpoint
levels.prompt: Find the flaw and the fix. (command injection — running attacker-chosen OS commands)
levels.hint: Untrusted input is being handed to the operating system. What could `host` contain besides a hostname?

fixes.label: Validate host against a strict allowlist / hostname pattern, and don't invoke a shell — pass args to the exe directly
Escape spaces in host before running it

levels.explain: Building a shell command from user input is command injection: host = "x & del /q C:\\*" runs the attacker's command too. Never pass untrusted input through a shell (cmd.exe /c). Validate it against a strict allowlist/pattern and invoke the program directly with separated arguments.

failStates.title: The log line isn't the flaw
failStates.explain: Logging the value is fine (a fixed message template). The flaw is feeding untrusted input to a shell.

failStates.title: Escaping a shell is a losing game
failStates.explain: Shell escaping is notoriously easy to get wrong. Don't invoke a shell with user input at all — allowlist the value and call the exe with explicit arguments.

failStates.title: It's not just ping
failStates.explain: Through cmd.exe, the attacker can chain any command (& del …, | powershell …). This is a full remote-code-execution hole.

levels.title: L3 · The login redirect
levels.prompt: Find the flaw and the fix. (open redirect — bouncing users to an attacker's site)
levels.hint: After login it redirects to a URL from the request. What if that URL points somewhere off your site?

payload.intro: After a successful login, send the user back where they came from.

fixes.label: Only redirect to local URLs — check Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl), else send to a safe default

levels.explain: An open redirect lets an attacker craft a link on YOUR trusted domain (…/login?returnUrl=https://evil.example) that bounces the victim to a malicious site after login — great for phishing. Only redirect to URLs that stay on your own site: guard with Url.IsLocalUrl and fall back to a safe default.

failStates.title: Encoding doesn't limit the destination
failStates.explain: HTML-encoding is for output, not for deciding where a redirect goes. You need to reject non-local URLs.

failStates.title: Signing in isn't the flaw
failStates.explain: The login itself is fine. The flaw is redirecting to an unchecked, attacker-supplied URL.
